name: Zaccharie Risacher
notes: A French wing who developed through ASVEL's academy and a JL Bourg loan (10.1/3.8 in 22 minutes, EuroCup Rising Star, LNB Élite Best Young Player), real two-way size and shooting from a proven European pathway, son of an Olympic silver medalist. Atlanta took him 1st, the second straight French No. 1 pick after Wembanyama. Risacher's rookie year was solid (12.6 ppg, a 38-point game) before a dip to 9.6 ppg in a reduced 2025-26 role and a July 2026 trade to Dallas. Solid outcome: real two-way tools that have produced a steady if unspectacular rotation role rather than a clear star trajectory so far.

name: Alex Sarr
notes: A French big man who trained at Real Madrid before Overtime Elite and a season with Australia's Perth Wildcats (9.4/4.3/1.5 blk), elite rim-protecting and stretch-five upside from an unconventional path. Washington took him 2nd. Sarr won Rookie of the Month honors and made the All-Rookie First Team (13.0/6.5/1.5 blk), then broke out further in 2025-26 (16.3/7.4/2.7, a 34-point game) before foot surgery in June 2026. Hit: real, ready-made two-way big-man tools that have translated directly into a genuine ascending NBA starter.

name: Reed Sheppard
notes: A four-star Kentucky freshman whose statistical profile was historically elite (12.5/4.5/4.1 on a remarkable 53.6/52.1% shooting), SEC Freshman of the Year and a unanimous "best shooter in the class" evaluation. Houston took him 3rd. Sheppard's rookie role stayed limited (4.4 ppg, a brief G League assignment) before a real 2025-26 breakout — 13.5/3.4/2.9 across 21 starts, a 31-point game, a 9-three-pointer game. Hit: elite shooting efficiency that, once given real minutes, became a genuine, ascending NBA guard.

name: Stephon Castle
notes: UConn's Big East Freshman of the Year on the 2024 national title team (11.1/4.7/2.9 on 47.2% shooting), real size-and-versatility guard upside from a champion. San Antonio took him 4th. Castle won unanimous Rookie of the Year (14.7/4.1/3.7, All-Rookie First Team), then took a full leap in 2025-26 — 16.7/7.4 with four triple-doubles, a 40-point game, and an 18.2 ppg playoff run to the 2026 Finals. Hit: exactly the emerging-star trajectory projected, arriving ahead of schedule.

name: Ron Holland
notes: A G League Ignite five-star who turned down Texas (18.5/6.7/2.8/2.1 stl before a thumb injury ended his season), elite recruiting pedigree and athleticism on a non-college path. Detroit took him 5th. Holland settled into steady, real rookie production (6.4/2.7) and continued growth in his second season (8.2/4.0 across 78 games). Solid outcome: real athletic talent developing into a genuine, growing NBA rotation piece, short of his top-five draft billing so far.

name: Tidjane Salaün
notes: A French forward who broke out at Cholet (9.6/3.9/1.0 stl in LNB Élite and FIBA Champions League, MVP of the 2023 Trophée du Futur at 17.7/7.3), real long-term upside as part of a historic three-Frenchmen top-10 run (with Risacher and Sarr). Charlotte took him 6th. Salaün's early NBA production stayed modest (5.9/4.7, then 6.0/4.0 in a reduced role) with real G League time (a 2026 championship with Greensboro). Mixed outcome: real long-term upside still translating slowly into consistent NBA production.

name: Donovan Clingan
notes: A two-time UConn national champion and dominant high school scorer-rebounder-shot-blocker (30.3/18.4/6.2 as a senior) who came off the bench for two Huskies title runs, elite size and rim protection from a winning program. Portland took him 7th, wearing No. 23 after his college No. 32 was retired for Bill Walton. Clingan led all rookies in blocks (All-Rookie Second Team) and developed into a full-time starter in 2025-26 — 12.1/11.6/1.7 blk, leading the NBA in offensive rebounds. Hit: elite winning-program size and defense that became a genuine, dominant young NBA starting center.

name: Rob Dillingham
notes: A five-star Kentucky freshman and SEC Sixth Man of the Year (15.2/3.9 on 47.5/44.4% shooting), elite instant-offense scoring and shot-making off the bench. San Antonio took him 8th (traded to Minnesota). Dillingham's early Wolves role stayed marginal (4.5, then 3.5 ppg, real G League time) before a February 2026 trade to Chicago (part of a deal involving Ayo Dosunmu and Julian Phillips) unlocked real production — 9.6/2.8/3.0 across 30 games before wrist surgery. Mixed outcome: real shot-creation talent that needed a change of scenery to find genuine NBA minutes.

name: Zach Edey
notes: Purdue's two-time unanimous National Player of the Year and two-time Big Ten Player of the Year (18.2/9.6 career, a 25.2 ppg senior season, 2,516 career points), the most decorated college big man in a generation, size and rebounding many questioned would translate given below-average NBA-level mobility. Memphis took him 9th. Edey won All-Rookie First Team honors immediately (9.2/8.3/1.3 blk, a 21-rebound franchise-rookie-record game) and improved further (13.6/11.1 in limited 2025-26 action) before an ankle injury (surgery, then reinjury) sidelined him. Hit: dominant, historic college production translating into a genuine productive NBA center, health the recurring question.

name: Cody Williams
notes: A consensus five-star Colorado freshman and McDonald's All-American (11.9/3.0, Pac-12 All-Freshman), real long-term wing upside on a limited one-year role, younger brother of Jalen Williams. Utah took him 10th. Williams's rookie chance stayed marginal (4.6/2.3) before real growth in 2025-26 (8.8/3.0, 41 starts, a 34-point game) — though also a historically bad single-game plus-minus (-60) — leading to an August 2026 trade to Minnesota. Mixed outcome: real developmental growth, though still finding a settled NBA role.

name: Matas Buzelis
notes: A five-star G League Ignite product (14.1/6.6/1.9, a Rising Stars selection) whose pre-draft buzz reached top-five range before a fall to 11th, elite recruiting-era wing upside on modest non-college stats. Chicago took him 11th. Buzelis started immediately (8.6 ppg, All-Rookie Second Team, first Lithuanian in the Slam Dunk Contest) then took a full leap as a full-time starter in 2025-26 — 16.3/5.8, a 41-point game, becoming Chicago's leading scorer after midseason trades. Hit: real recruiting-era upside that developed rapidly into a genuine ascending NBA lead scorer.

name: Nikola Topić
notes: A Serbian point guard who debuted for Crvena zvezda at 16 and became ABA League Top Prospect (17.9/6.8/3.6, FIBA U18 European Championship MVP, two ABA titles), elite feel and pedigree undercut right before the draft by a partially torn ACL suffered in the 2024 ABA Finals. Oklahoma City took him 12th. Topić missed his entire rookie season recovering from surgery, was then diagnosed with testicular cancer in October 2025 during his recovery, and made his NBA debut in February 2026 (5.2/4.4/1.9 in 10 games) — still earning a 2025 championship ring despite never playing that season. Mixed outcome: elite pre-draft talent whose NBA start has been defined almost entirely by serious injury and illness rather than production so far.

name: Devin Carter
notes: A South Carolina-to-Providence riser and Big East Player of the Year as a senior (nearly 20/9 with elite defensive motor, First-Team All-Big East), real two-way development from a mid-major breakout. Sacramento took him 13th. Carter's rookie role stayed limited (3.8/2.1) before real growth in 2025-26 (8.9/3.3 across 12 starts, a 29-point/6-three game) — a June 2026 trade sent him to Atlanta. Solid outcome: real two-way college development translating into steady, growing NBA production.

name: Bub Carrington
notes: A Pitt freshman who opened his college career with the program's first-ever triple-double (13.8/5.2/4.1, ACC All-Rookie), real all-around guard feel from day one. Portland took him 14th (traded to Washington with Malcolm Brogdon for Deni Avdija). Carrington started immediately (9.8/4.2/4.4 across all 82 games, All-Rookie Second Team) and grew further (10.7/3.4/4.6), becoming the first player since Karl-Anthony Towns to play every game in each of his first two seasons. Hit: real, immediate all-around guard production that has held steady across two full, durable NBA seasons.

name: Kel'el Ware
notes: An Oregon-to-Indiana transfer whose disappointing freshman year (6.6/4.1, work-ethic concerns) gave way to a Second-Team All-Big Ten breakout (15.9/9.9, All-Defensive), elite physical tools that took a year to translate into production. Miami took him 15th. Ware won All-Rookie Second Team honors (9.3/7.4/1.1 blk) and grew further (11.1/9.0/1.1, a historic 10-10-5-5 bench game) before a July 2026 blockbuster trade to Milwaukee (the Giannis deal). Hit: real physical upside that, once he found consistency, became a genuine productive NBA big man.

name: Jared McCain
notes: A five-star Duke freshman (14.3/5.0, a 35-point game tying Zion Williamson's freshman record, ACC All-Rookie), elite shooting and scoring instincts. Philadelphia took him 16th. McCain won Rookie of the Month honors early (16.0 ppg) before a meniscus tear ended his rookie season; a thumb UCL surgery further limited 2025-26 (6.6 ppg) before a February 2026 trade to Oklahoma City unlocked real production — 10.4 ppg in the regular season and a Western Conference Finals playoff run. Mixed outcome: real shooting talent whose early NBA years have been defined as much by injury as by the star potential originally scouted.

name: Dalton Knecht
notes: An unconventional junior-college-to-Northern Colorado-to-Tennessee graduate transfer whose final season was a genuine breakout (21.7 ppg, unanimous SEC Player of the Year, consensus First-Team All-American, a 40-point senior night), elite, proven scoring from an older, well-traveled prospect. LA Lakers took him 17th. Knecht delivered immediately (9.1 ppg, a 37-point/9-three rookie game tying the rookie record) before a sharp 2025-26 decline to a G League-heavy role (4.2 ppg). Bust relative to his college scoring pedigree, after a genuinely strong rookie debut.

name: Tristan Da Silva
notes: A four-year Colorado riser who broke out as a First-Team All-Pac-12 junior (15.9/4.8/1.3 stl) before an even better senior season (16.0/5.1/2.4, Second-Team All-Pac-12), real patient, well-rounded wing development. Orlando took him 18th. Da Silva developed steadily in his first two NBA seasons (7.2 to 9.9 ppg, improved shooting to 45.0/37.4%). Solid outcome: real, patient college development translating into steady, improving NBA production.

name: Ja'Kobe Walter
notes: A five-star Baylor freshman who set the program's freshman-debut scoring record (14.5/4.4/1.4, Big 12 Freshman of the Year), real scoring instincts on modest efficiency (37.6/34.1%). Toronto took him 19th. Walter delivered real rookie production (8.6 ppg, a game-winning three) and continued as a genuine rotation piece in 2025-26 (7.5 ppg on much-improved 40.9% three-point shooting), including a strong playoff stretch (11.1 ppg, a 24-point overtime game). Solid outcome: real recruiting-era scoring talent settling into a genuine, improving NBA rotation role.

name: Jaylon Tyson
notes: A three-school journey (Texas, then Texas Tech, then Cal after citing a coach's racist comments) that culminated in a First-Team All-Pac-12 senior breakout (19.6/3.5 ast), real late-blooming scoring production from an unusually well-traveled path. Cleveland took him 20th. Tyson's rookie role stayed marginal (3.6/2.0, heavy G League time) before a full 2025-26 breakout — 13.2/5.1/2.2 across 42 starts, a 39-point game with the game-winning assist to Evan Mobley. Hit: real late-blooming college scoring that became a genuine, ascending NBA rotation player in his second season.

name: Yves Missi
notes: A Baylor freshman ranked ESPN's third-best center nationally (10.7/5.6/1.5 blk on an elite 61.4% FG in limited minutes, Big 12 All-Defensive and All-Freshman), real, efficient rim-running upside. New Orleans took him 21st. Missi started immediately and won All-Rookie Second Team honors (9.1/8.2, 54.7% FG, 67 starts) before a reduced 2025-26 role (5.7/5.8 across 66 games, 14 starts). Solid outcome: real rookie-year production that took a step back in year two, still a genuine NBA rotation big.

name: DaRon Holmes
notes: Dayton's Atlantic 10 co-Player of the Year as a junior (20.4/8.5/2.1 blk, consensus Second-Team All-American, a school-record 81 blocks as a freshman), elite, proven college production across three seasons. Phoenix took him 22nd (traded to Denver). A torn Achilles suffered in Summer League — just three days after signing — wiped out his entire rookie season; he debuted in October 2025 and has managed only modest, G League-supplemented minutes since (3.7/1.4 across 25 games). Bust so far: elite college production that a serious injury has kept almost entirely from NBA opportunity.

name: AJ Johnson
notes: A late-rising 2023 guard recruit (a dramatic pandemic-era growth spurt from 5'10" to 6'5") who skipped college for Australia's NBL Next Stars, real long-term upside on very thin direct production (2.9/1.3/0.7 in limited NBL minutes). Milwaukee took him 23rd, a widely-criticized "reach" pick. Johnson has been traded three times (Washington, Dallas, Memphis, then New Orleans) in under two years, never securing more than marginal minutes (4.9 ppg career). Bust: thin pre-draft production translating into an equally thin, well-traveled NBA path so far.

name: Kyshawn George
notes: A three-star Miami freshman who became a starter mid-season due to injuries (7.6/3.0/2.2 on strong 42.6/40.8% shooting), real shooting efficiency on a modest recruiting profile and thin role. New York took him 24th (immediately traded to Washington). George set a Wizards rookie three-point record (8.7/4.2/2.5, All-Rookie-caliber debut) and took a real leap in 2025-26 — 14.8/5.1/4.5, a 34-point/11-rebound game — before a partial UCL tear in his elbow ended his season in March 2026. Hit: real shooting efficiency that developed rapidly into a genuine breakout NBA starter, interrupted by injury.

name: Pacôme Dadiet
notes: A French wing who developed through Paris Basketball and Germany's Bundesliga (Ratiopharm Ulm), part of a historic four-Frenchman first-round class, real long-term two-way upside on modest direct production. New York took him 25th. Dadiet has barely played across two Knicks seasons (1.7 ppg in 5.3 minutes) but has won two championships in a bench/depth role — the 2025 NBA Cup and the 2026 NBA Finals over San Antonio. Bust in terms of on-court development so far, though a genuine multi-time champion.

name: Dillon Jones
notes: Weber State's four-year Big Sky Player of the Year (20.8/9.8/5.2 as a senior, three-time First-Team All-Big Sky), real all-around production from a mid-major star. Washington took him 26th (traded to Oklahoma City). Jones has bounced extensively — heavy G League time with OKC (winning the 2025 championship in a bench role), a trade to Washington and waiver, a G League draft selection, and a two-way Knicks signing that produced a second championship ring in 2026 — without ever securing real NBA minutes. Bust in terms of NBA playing time, though a genuine two-time champion by circumstance.

name: Terrence Shannon Jr.
notes: A Texas Tech-to-Illinois transfer whose senior breakout was historic (23.0 ppg, Big Ten Tournament Most Outstanding Player, multiple Illinois scoring records, Third-Team All-American), elite go-to college scoring from an experienced, four-year path. Minnesota took him 27th. Shannon's NBA role has stayed limited through two seasons (5.1 ppg, heavy G League time) with a real 2026 playoff flash (a 24-point playoff-starting-debut game). Mixed outcome: real college scoring pedigree that has yet to translate into a settled NBA role, though flashes of postseason production have emerged.

name: Ryan Dunn
notes: Virginia's sophomore breakout and widely regarded "best defensive player in the class" (8.1/6.9/2.3 blk/1.3 stl on 54.8% FG), elite defensive versatility on a still-developing offensive game. Denver took him 28th (traded to Phoenix). Dunn earned a starting role by January of his rookie year (6.9/3.6, a first double-double) and continued as a real Suns rotation piece in 2025-26 (5.8/4.2, improved 33.1% three-point shooting). Solid outcome: elite defensive tools translating into a genuine, developing NBA starting-caliber role.

name: Isaiah Collier
notes: USC's five-star, ESPN and Rivals No. 1 overall 2023 recruit (16.3/4.3/1.5 stl, Naismith Prep Player of the Year in high school), elite point-guard pedigree. Utah took him 29th. Collier became the Jazz's starting point guard by late January of his rookie year (8.7/6.3/3.3, a Jazz rookie-record 10 assists in a half) and broke out further in 2025-26 (11.7/7.2 on improved 49.5% shooting, a 22-assist game — the most by a Jazz player since John Stockton). Hit: elite college point-guard pedigree developing exactly as projected into a genuine ascending NBA floor general.

name: Baylor Scheierman
notes: A South Dakota State-to-Creighton riser who capped his career with a unanimous First-Team All-Big East senior season (18.5/9.0/3.9, multiple All-America honors), real, proven all-around production across two mid-major-to-high-major stops. Boston took him 30th. Scheierman's rookie role stayed marginal (3.6 ppg, heavy G League time) before a real 2025-26 expanded role (5.5/3.5 across 20 starts, 39.9% from three) — Boston exercised his 2026-27 team option. Solid outcome: real, patient development into a genuine, retained NBA rotation piece.

name: Jonathan Mogbo
notes: A four-school journey (Independence CC, Northeastern Oklahoma A&M, Missouri State, then San Francisco) that culminated in a First-Team All-WCC breakout senior season (14.2/10.1 on 63.6% FG, WCC Newcomer of the Year), real all-around production from an unconventional, late-blooming path. Toronto took him 31st. Mogbo delivered a real rookie role (6.2/4.9/2.3, a triple-double) before a sharp 2025-26 decline (1.5/1.7) and a 2026 two-way signing with Sacramento. Mixed outcome: a promising rookie debut that has not yet been sustained.

name: Kyle Filipowski
notes: Duke's ACC Rookie of the Year (15.1/9.0, 16 double-doubles) who followed with a First-Team All-ACC sophomore season (16.4/8.3, a 30-point game) despite an offseason hip surgery, elite, proven production across two Duke seasons. Utah took him 32nd. Filipowski has been a real, steady NBA contributor across two seasons — 10.5/6.7 on strong 49.6/33.7% shooting through 149 games. Hit: real two-year college production that has translated directly into a genuine, productive NBA big man.

name: Tyler Smith
notes: A top-20 2023 recruit (Kansas, Baylor and Texas offers) who chose Overtime Elite and later G League Ignite over college, real long-term wing upside (15.7/8.0/1.9 stl/1.3 blk in his final OTE year) from a non-traditional path. Milwaukee took him 33rd. Smith's NBA chance has stayed almost entirely marginal — a Bucks waiver, brief Houston and Dallas two-way stints (2.9 to 4.7 ppg) — before a July 2026 release left him a free agent. Bust: real recruiting-era athletic upside that thin opportunity across three organizations never let develop into NBA production.

name: Tyler Kolek
notes: A George Mason-to-Marquette riser and Big East Player of the Year (15.3/7.7, leading the NCAA in assists, consensus Second-Team All-American), elite college playmaking pedigree. Portland took him 34th (traded to New York on draft night). Kolek's NBA role has stayed largely G League-supplemented (2.0, then 4.4 ppg) but he's won both the 2025 NBA Cup and the 2026 championship over San Antonio as a Knicks reserve. Bust in terms of NBA playing time, though a genuine multi-time champion.

name: Johnny Furphy
notes: A Kansas freshman whose lone college season showed real shooting and rebounding flashes (9.0/4.9 on 46.6% FG, a 23-point/11-rebound game, Big 12 All-Freshman), a notably young, one-year Australian prospect. San Antonio took him 35th (traded to Indiana). Furphy's rookie role stayed marginal (2.1 ppg) before real 2025-26 growth (5.2/4.4 across 21 starts, a 17-point game) — a torn right ACL in February 2026 ended his season. Mixed outcome: real developmental growth cut short by a serious knee injury.

name: Juan Nunez
notes: A Real Madrid academy product and 2019-20 EuroLeague Next Generation Tournament MVP (9.5/5.0), then a German Bundesliga champion with Ratiopharm Ulm (9.0/5.0 in EuroCup), real, proven European point-guard pedigree. Indiana took him 36th (traded to San Antonio), but the Spurs never signed him — Núñez instead joined FC Barcelona on a three-year deal in 2024. Never played in the NBA — a real, accomplished young EuroLeague playmaker who chose Europe over an NBA contract.

name: Bobi Klintman
notes: A Swedish forward whose lone Wake Forest season was modest (5.3/4.5), before he withdrew from the 2023 draft to play Australia's NBL Next Stars program (9.7/4.8 with Cairns), real long-term developmental upside on thin production. Minnesota took him 37th (traded to Detroit with Wendell Moore Jr.). Klintman barely played across two Pistons seasons (20 total games, 1.9/1.3), heavy G League time, before an April 2026 waiver and a July 2026 signing with Italy's Virtus Bologna. Bust: real physical upside that thin NBA opportunity never let develop into consistent production.

name: Ajay Mitchell
notes: A three-year UC Santa Barbara riser and Big West Player of the Year as a sophomore, capped by a First-Team All-Big West junior season (20.0/4.0/4.0, 16.1 career ppg on 51.1% FG), real, proven mid-major scoring and playmaking development. New York took him 38th (traded to Oklahoma City). Mitchell won a 2025 championship as a rookie (6.5/1.8/1.9, a turf-toe injury requiring surgery) before a real 2025-26 breakout — 13.6/3.6/3.3 across 16 starts, a 28-point playoff game — re-signing for $9M. Hit: real mid-major production that developed into a genuine, well-paid NBA rotation player and champion.

name: Jaylen Wells
notes: A Division II Sonoma State CCAA Player of the Year (22.4 ppg) who transferred up to Washington State for one Division I season (12.6/4.6), real, late-emerging scoring instincts from an unusual two-tier college path. Memphis took him 39th. Wells delivered immediately (10.4/3.4/1.7 across 74 starts, All-Rookie First Team, Rookie of the Month) before a broken wrist ended his rookie year; he returned to a full 69-start 2025-26 season (12.5/3.2/1.6) before a season-ending toe surgery in March 2026. Hit: real, rapid development from a Division II background into a genuine NBA starter, injuries a recurring interruption.

name: Oso Ighodaro
notes: Marquette's Second-Team All-Big East senior and Academic All-American (13.4/6.9/3.3, elite two-way feel and passing for a big man). Portland took him 40th (traded to Phoenix). Ighodaro developed steadily from a limited rookie role (4.2/3.6 on 60.4% FG) into a full-time 2025-26 contributor (6.5/5.1/2.3 across 24 starts, all 82 games) with real 2026 playoff minutes. Solid outcome: real passing-big feel translating into a genuine, growing NBA rotation role.

name: Adem Bona
notes: UCLA's back-to-back Pac-12 Freshman of the Year and Defensive Player of the Year (12.4/5.9 as a sophomore on 58.8% FG, 115 career blocks), elite rim protection undercut by chronic foul trouble. Philadelphia took him 41st. Bona has developed into a real, efficient Sixers rotation big (5.8 to 4.8 ppg on 70%+ shooting) with real 2026 playoff minutes. Solid outcome: elite college defensive production translating into a genuine, efficient NBA rotation role.

name: KJ Simpson
notes: Colorado's First-Team All-Pac-12 junior breakout (19.7 ppg on 43% from three, a buzzer-beating NCAA Tournament game-winner against Florida), real go-to scoring development across three seasons. Charlotte took him 42nd. Simpson's rookie role showed real promise (7.8/3.0/3.1 across 15 starts) before a 2026 waiver and a Denver two-way signing produced only marginal minutes since. Mixed outcome: a promising rookie debut that has not yet been sustained into a settled NBA role.

name: Nikola Djurisic
notes: A Serbian wing (Mega Basket academy) and ABA League Top Prospect (14.4/3.4/2.7 in ABA League play, a 2022 EuroLeague Next Generation Tournament Finals MVP), real international pedigree. Miami took him 43rd (traded to Atlanta). Đurišić never made an NBA roster — G League time with Atlanta's affiliate, a 2025 Hawks signing that didn't stick — before a 2026 move to Serbian powerhouse Crvena zvezda (loaned to Mega Basket). Bust at the NBA level, a real, still-developing prospect back in Serbia's top league.

name: Pelle Larsson
notes: A Utah-to-Arizona transfer and Pac-12 Sixth Man of the Year turned Second-Team All-Pac-12 senior (12.8/4.1), real, steady college scoring development. Houston took him 44th (traded to Miami). Larsson has developed into a genuine Heat rotation piece across two seasons — 8.4/2.7/2.4 career, a real 2025-26 breakout to 11.4 ppg on 49.6% shooting across 54 starts. Hit: real, patient college development translating into a genuine, improving NBA starter.

name: Jamal Shead
notes: Houston's Big 12 Player and Defensive Player of the Year in the same season (12.9/6.3/2.2 stl, consensus First-Team All-American, Naismith and NABC Defensive Player of the Year), elite winning-program point-guard defense and playmaking. Sacramento took him 45th (traded to Toronto). Shead earned real rookie minutes as Toronto's third-string point guard (7.1/4.2, second among rookies in franchise assists) before a full 2025-26 season (6.6/5.4, career highs of 22 points/13 assists). Hit: elite college two-way point-guard production translating into a genuine, developing NBA role.

name: Cam Christie
notes: A Minnesota freshman whose lone college season showed real shooting efficiency (11.3/3.6/2.2 on 40.3/39.1% shooting, Big Ten All-Freshman, an 18-point debut). LA Clippers took him 46th. Christie's NBA chance has stayed almost entirely marginal — heavy G League time across two seasons, growing modestly from 1.4 to 2.8 ppg in limited minutes. Bust so far: real freshman shooting efficiency that thin opportunity has kept from translating into NBA production.

name: Antonio Reeves
notes: An Illinois State-to-Kentucky riser whose fifth (COVID) season was a genuine breakout (20.2 ppg on elite 51.2/44.7% shooting, Third-Team All-American, First-Team All-SEC), real efficient high-volume scoring from an experienced, well-traveled college path. Orlando took him 47th (traded to New Orleans). Reeves showed real flashes (6.9 ppg, a 34-point birthday game) before a 2025 waiver and a Charlotte two-way signing produced only marginal minutes since (2.7 ppg). Mixed outcome: real efficient scoring shown in flashes, not yet a settled NBA role.

name: Harrison Ingram
notes: A consensus five-star recruit whose college path spanned Stanford (Pac-12 Freshman of the Year, 10.5/6.7) and North Carolina (12.2/8.8, Third-Team All-ACC), real size-and-rebounding versatility across two high-major stops. San Antonio took him 48th. Ingram's NBA chance has stayed almost entirely theoretical (12 total games across two seasons, 1.3 ppg) before a July 2026 release and a signing with Utah. Bust: real recruiting-era, multi-program college production that has yet to find any real NBA opportunity.

name: Tristen Newton
notes: A four-year, two-school (East Carolina, then UConn) winning college star who led back-to-back national championships and earned the 2024 Bob Cousy Award and consensus First-Team All-American honors as a two-time NCAA Tournament Most Outstanding Player-caliber leader, elite winning production and playmaking from an experienced, decorated path. Indiana took him 49th. Newton's NBA chance has stayed almost entirely marginal — a Pacers waiver, a scoreless Minnesota stint, a 2026 Houston two-way signing (9 total career games, 1.7 ppg). Bust: an unusually decorated college winner whose NBA opportunity has never materialized.

name: Enrique Freeman
notes: A former walk-on who grew four inches in college and became Akron's MAC Player of the Year and the NCAA's national rebounding leader as a senior (14.0/10.6 career, 12.9 rpg as a senior, MAC Defensive Player of the Year and Tournament MVP as a junior), an extraordinary underdog college story built on elite rebounding. Indiana took him 50th. Freeman's NBA chance has stayed marginal across two two-way stints (Indiana, then Minnesota) — 2.1 to 3.3 ppg in limited G League-heavy minutes. Bust so far at the NBA level, though a genuinely inspiring college rebounding story.

name: Melvin Ajinça
notes: A French wing who developed through Centre Fédéral and Saint-Quentin (9.7/3.3, All-Tournament at the 2023 FIBA U19 World Cup Final, 19.3 ppg in that tournament), real long-term two-way upside on modest direct production. New York took him 51st (traded to Dallas). Ajinça's draft rights were traded back to New York in a 2026 five-team deal without ever signing an NBA contract. Never played in the NBA — a real developmental prospect still finding his path to a roster spot.

name: Quinten Post
notes: A Mississippi State-to-Boston College riser and Second-Team All-ACC senior (17.0/8.1 on elite 51.4/43.1% shooting, ACC Most Improved Player the year prior), a Dutch stretch-five with real, proven shooting efficiency from a late-blooming path. Golden State took him 52nd, the first Dutch player drafted since 2009. Post developed into a genuine rotation piece (7.8/3.8 across 109 games, a 20-point game) before a July 2026 offer sheet from Memphis (Golden State declined to match). Hit: real shooting-big efficiency that became a genuine NBA rotation contributor.

name: Cam Spencer
notes: A three-school (Loyola Maryland, Rutgers, UConn), five-year veteran who won a 2024 national title as First-Team All-Big East and Academic All-American (14.2/4.3/3.3 career, 11 points in the championship game), elite, proven shooting and winning feel from an unusually experienced path. Detroit took him 53rd (traded to Memphis). Spencer needed a quiet rookie year (4.2 ppg, a 51-point G League game) before a real 2025-26 breakout — 11.1/5.6 across 20 starts, a 27-point/6-assist game — earning a four-year, $10.5M extension. Hit: proven, experienced college shooting and feel that became a genuine, well-paid NBA rotation player.

name: Anton Watson
notes: A five-year Gonzaga forward whose senior season was his best — First-Team All-WCC (14.5/7.1 on an elite 58.6% career FG) after early shoulder surgery limited his freshman year — real, patient, winning-program development. Boston took him 54th. Watson's NBA chance has stayed almost entirely marginal — a Celtics waiver, brief Knicks (9 games) and Lakers stints — currently in the G League with Coachella Valley. Bust: real, efficient college production that has yet to find any lasting NBA opportunity.

name: Bronny James
notes: LeBron James's son, whose lone USC season was limited both statistically (4.8/2.8/2.1) and by a cardiac arrest suffered in a July 2023 practice that delayed his college debut, real recruiting-era hype clouded by a serious health scare right before his draft year. LA Lakers took him 55th, making LeBron and Bronny the first active father-son duo in NBA history. Bronny's role has grown gradually (2.3, then 2.9 ppg on improved shooting) and in April 2026 he and LeBron became the first father-son duo to play in a playoff game together. Bust in terms of pure production, though a genuine, historic NBA milestone and a real, gradually developing role.

name: Kevin McCullar Jr.
notes: A Texas Tech-to-Kansas transfer whose senior breakout was real (18.3 ppg, First-Team All-Big 12, Third-Team All-American), elite, proven wing scoring and defense from an experienced college path. Phoenix took him 56th (traded to New York). McCullar's NBA chance has stayed almost entirely marginal (4 then 21 games, 1.5 to 2.4 ppg) but he won the 2026 championship over San Antonio as part of the Knicks' title run. Bust in terms of NBA minutes, though a genuine champion.

name: Ulrich Chomche
notes: The first Basketball Africa League player ever drafted into the NBA — ESPN called him "the best Cameroonian prospect since Joel Embiid" — a 6'11", 7'4"-wingspan defensive prospect (BAL production of 2.1-4.5/3.7-4.8) with a still-developing offensive game. Memphis took him 57th (traded to Toronto), the youngest player in the draft. Chomche's NBA chance was cut almost immediately short — 7 games (0.7/1.1) before a partial MCL tear ended his season, and a 2025 waiver sent him to Bulgaria's Balkan Botevgrad. Bust: elite defensive-prospect pedigree that a serious knee injury never let develop into real NBA opportunity.

name: Ariel Hukporti
notes: A German-Togolese big man who developed through Riesen Ludwigsburg and Lithuania before a torn Achilles in Australia's NBL (Melbourne United), real long-term rim-protecting upside interrupted by a serious injury before the draft. Dallas took him 58th, the draft's final pick (traded to New York). Hukporti showed real efficient flashes as a rookie (1.9/2.0 on 67.7% FG) before a torn meniscus, then a genuine role in the Knicks' 2026 championship run (a key block in a 29-point Finals Game 4 comeback) — signing with Philadelphia for $3.4M in 2026. Solid outcome: real, efficient rim-protecting production and a genuine championship contribution from Mr. Irrelevant.
